* This is called in the context of udc_ep_enable() or udc_ep_enable_internal(),
* the latter of which may be used by the driver to enable control endpoints.
* may be used by the driver to disable control endpoints.
/* Halt endpoint. Halted endpoint should respond with a STALL handshake. */
* A UDC driver should always be implemented as a multi-instance

claude.label: not_applicable
claude.label_text: Fix does not apply to the copy
claude.evidence: Two of the three picked hunks only rename: udc_dwc2_ep_enable/udc_dwc2_ep_disable become udc_dwc2_ep_activate/udc_dwc2_ep_deactivate and the API table is updated, because, as the commit message says, "The Zephyr USB device stack endpoint enable/disable refers to DWC2 activate/deactivate". The behavioural part (the middle hunk) adds a new DWC2-only udc_dwc2_ep_disable(dev, cfg, stall) that programs DCTL SGOUTNAK, GINTSTS GOUTNAKEFF and DxEPCTL EPENA/EPDIS/STALL/SNAK bits defined in drivers/usb/common/usb_dwc2_hw.h, which the fixed driver now calls from udc_dwc2_ep_set_halt. udc_skeleton.c matches only by the function names: its header says it is "a skeleton for a device controller driver using the UDC API", its ep_enable and ep_disable callbacks only call LOG_DBG and return 0 (lines 137-155), it touches no registers anywhere, and its set_halt only sets cfg->stat.halted. There is no DWC2 controller or pre-fix DWC2 register sequence on the skeleton side, so neither the rename (its ep_enable/ep_disable already mean the stack's enable/disable) nor the DWC2 STALL sequence applies.

Several NXP drivers require clock control subsystem name definition in
Devicetree. It prevents usage of clock control without subsystem such

claude.evidence: The listed hunks are the core of the ATCSPI200 fix: transceive() now sizes a full-duplex transfer with MAX(rx_len, tx_len) instead of MIN, and the DMA callbacks decide whether to reload from exact remaining frame counters (data->rx_cnt/tx_cnt) instead of spi_context_rx_on/tx_on, because, as the commit message says, "the transmission and reception counts must be consistent. If there is a mismatch in length, dummy data needs to be transmitted or received"; the block_idx-to-block_count resets in the error and END paths belong to the same DMA chain rework. spi_egis_et171.c is a copy of the pre-fix driver for the same IP (its binding says "based on the Andes ATCSPI200 architecture", and its header has the same register map and TRNS_MODE_WRITE_READ): transceive() still sets chunk_len = MIN(rx_len, tx_len) (line 681), spi_transfer() and spi_transfer_dma() write that one count to both SPI_WR_TRANS_CNT and SPI_RD_TRANS_CNT, the IRQ handler stops feeding TX once tx_cnt reaches chunk_len and calls spi_context_complete on the END interrupt, and dma_rx_callback/dma_tx_callback still test spi_context_rx_on/tx_on (lines 320 and 347). So any full-duplex call whose TX and RX totals differ (for example a 1-byte command followed by a longer read) clocks only the shorter length and returns success with the rest of the buffers never transferred, although spi.h says CS is held until all buffers in the provided buf sets have been transferred. Nothing in spi_egis_et171.c pads or splits such transfers, the fix needs only driver-local counters plus register macros and spi_context helpers that the ET171 side already has, and the chained-DMA line block_count = ctx->tx_count (line 434) that the same commit replaced is also still there (the ATCDMACx00 driver follows a chain only when block_count > 1). The ET171 file was reorganised (DMA block helper functions, DCACHE re-alignment of RX buffers), so the change has to be rewritten rather than copied; the commit's other edits that roll back API updates (DEVICE_API, error_callback_dis, SPI_DEVICE_DT_INST_DEFINE) are not part of the fix, since the fixed driver uses all three again today (lines 730, 897 and 972).

Egis ET171 SPI controller based on the Andes ATCSPI200 architecture.
the entire duration of the transfer of all buffers in the provided buf sets.

claude.title: The Egis ET171 SPI driver cuts full-duplex transfers down to the shorter of the TX and RX lengths, a bug already fixed in the Andes ATCSPI200 driver it was copied from.
claude.summary: The Andes ATCSPI200 SPI driver was fixed in commit f817f62021 (merged 2025-07-31): full-duplex transfers are now sized by MAX of the TX and RX lengths, with exact TX/RX frame counters so the shorter side is padded with dummy frames, because the IP needs equal write and read counts; the same commit also corrected how chained DMA blocks are counted. The Egis ET171 driver, whose binding and Kconfig say it is based on the ATCSPI200, was added on 2025-08-16 with the older code: transceive() still uses MIN(rx_len, tx_len), programs that one count into both transfer counters, and finishes the transaction at the END interrupt. A call such as a register-address write followed by a longer read therefore clocks only the shorter length and returns success, leaving the rest of the RX buffer unfilled (or the extra TX bytes unsent), and the DMA reload callbacks and chained block count still follow the old logic. Porting means reworking the interrupt handler and DMA loaders around the counters, not only changing MIN to MAX; note that at the pinned commit no in-tree devicetree defines an egis,et171-spi node, so the driver only runs when a board or overlay adds one.

The SPI burst read discarded 3 leading bytes, but the device's address
phase is only 2 bytes long, so every sample was shifted by one register.
Skip 2 bytes instead, matching the single-byte read and write paths.

Assisted-by: Claude:fable-5

claude.label: missing
claude.evidence: The fxos8700 commit says "The SPI burst read discarded 3 leading bytes, but the device's address phase is only 2 bytes long, so every sample was shifted by one register. Skip 2 bytes instead, matching the single-byte read and write paths." fxls8974_read_spi() in fxls8974.c is the same pre-fix code line for line (lines 41-47): it sends reg_buf[3] = { DIR_READ(reg), ADDR_7(reg), 0 } and uses that 3-byte buffer as the first RX entry, so the caller's data starts on the 4th byte. The same file's single-byte paths use a 2-byte address phase, exactly like fxos8700: fxls8974_byte_read_spi() clocks 3 bytes and returns data[2] (line 62) and fxls8974_byte_write_spi() sends the value as the 3rd byte (line 71); fxls8974_init() depends on that byte read to accept the WHOAMI value and to verify CTRL_REG4 after writing it (lines 517 and 544-549), so on a working SPI part the burst read is one register late. That burst read is what fxls8974_sample_fetch() uses for all accelerometer axes from FXLS8974_REG_OUTXLSB (line 272), so every SPI sample would be assembled from the wrong registers; nothing else in the driver compensates, and the fix uses only spi_buf/spi_buf_set and the DIR_READ/ADDR_7 macros that fxls8974.c already defines.

refs.quote: /* The address phase is 2 bytes; data starts on the 3rd byte. */

claude.title: The FXLS8974 accelerometer driver's SPI burst read skips one byte too many, so SPI samples are read one register late.
claude.summary: On 2026-09-24 the fxos8700 driver fixed its SPI burst read to skip only the 2-byte address phase instead of 3 bytes, matching its own single-byte read and write paths. fxls8974_read_spi() is a line-for-line copy of the old fxos8700 code and still discards 3 bytes, while the same driver's byte read takes the register value from the 3rd byte and its init relies on that to check WHOAMI and CTRL_REG4. With the sensor on SPI, sample_fetch's burst read of OUT_X_LSB onward therefore returns data starting one register later, so X, Y and Z are built from the wrong bytes (the I2C path is not affected). The fxos8700 change can be applied with only the names changed.

fix.subject: drivers/timer/it8xxx2: fix busy wait timer race condition
fix.message:
drivers/timer/it8xxx2: fix busy wait timer race condition

Command "waitms 50" on ChromeBook EC console, then it will crash EC.

Because arch_busy_wait() is re-entried by two different tasks,
the second calling will reset the timer and may cause the first
calling to fail to reach the waiting destination
(if the first calling's wait time is longer enough).

Verified by follow test pattern:
west build -p auto -b it8xxx2_evb tests/kernel/timer/timer_api
west build -p auto -b it8xxx2_evb tests/kernel/timer/timer_error_case
west build -p auto -b it8xxx2_evb tests/kernel/timer/timer_monotonic
west build -p auto -b it8xxx2_evb tests/kernel/timer/starve
west build -p auto -b it8xxx2_evb tests/kernel/context

Signed-off-by: Ruibin Chang <Ruibin.Chang@ite.com.tw>

lines: /* Decrease 1us here to calibrate our access registers latency */
* We want to set the bit(1) re-start busy wait timer as soon
* as possible, so we directly write 0xb instead of | bit(1).
* The EC runs at 9.2MHz, meaning each tick is approximately 108.6ns.
* The number of ticks per microsecond is calculated as:
* Since the timer counts down from a preset value to 0, using a preload value of
* 9 actually results in 10 ticks per cycle.
* This overestimates 1us and introduces a small cumulative timing error over time.
* To compensate for this, we scale the requested delay using (1000 / 1086).

claude.label: already_ok
claude.evidence: The fix addresses the commit message's race, "arch_busy_wait() is re-entried by two different tasks, the second calling will reset the timer": it removes the write of IT8XXX2_EXT_ETX_COMB_RST_EN that restarted the busy-wait timer on every call, records a start count at entry, and waits on the difference. In ite_it51xxx_timer.c, arch_busy_wait already reads start = read_timer_obser(BUSY_WAIT_H_TIMER) at entry and loops until the difference from start (read_timer_obser(...) - start in count-up mode, start - read_timer_obser(...) otherwise) reaches the wait time, and it writes no timer control register. The only writer of the reset bit TIMER_ETNRST is ext_timer_enable(), which at run time is called only for EVENT_TIMER (timer_driver_set_reload and evt_timer_isr); the busy-wait timers are started once in sys_clock_driver_init via timer_init. A second concurrent caller therefore cannot restart the counter under the first one, so the it51xxx copy never had this race.

fix.subject: drivers: clock_control: stm32h7: fix incorrect VCO configuration logic
fix.message:
drivers: clock_control: stm32h7: fix incorrect VCO configuration logic

There are two VCO parameters the driver configures: the input range
and the operation mode (VCOL/VCOH). While the two parameters may appear
independent, they are not because the valid input ranges depend on the
selected VCO mode, which itself depends on the target vco_ck frequency.
As such, the current logic which evaluates only refx_ck to determine the
input range and "deduces" the operation mode from input range is not
correct.

While we could keep two independent routines, it seems simpler to merge
both `get_vco_input_range()` and `get_vco_output_range()` into a single
`get_vco_parameters()` routine which computes both parameters from the
refx_ck and target vcox_ck (or returns an error if the configuration is
not legal) since separate routines, if preserved, would accept the same
parameters anyways.

While at it, take advantage of the new st,vcoh-frequency-range property
to ensure the legal configuration evaluation is valid on a per-product
basis.

Signed-off-by: Mathieu Choplain <mathieu.choplain-ext@st.com>

lines: /* Given source clock and dividers, compute the output frequency of PLLx_P */
static int get_vco_parameters(uint32_t ref_ck, uint32_t target_vco_ck,
* Some constraints are consistent across all lines of STM32H7 SoCs:
* - In VCOL mode: 1 MHz <= ref_ck <= 2 MHz, 150 MHz <= vco_ck <= 420 MHz
* - In VCOH mode: 2 MHz <= ref_ck <= 16 MHz
* Constraints on vco_ck when operating in VCOH mode vary depending on the
* product line and are taken from DT. Refer to figure "PLL block diagram"
* or section "PLL description" of RM0399, RM0433, RM0455, RM0468 and RM0477
const bool vcol_input_ok = IN_RANGE(ref_ck, MHZ(1), MHZ(2));
const bool vcol_output_ok = IN_RANGE(target_vco_ck, MHZ(150), MHZ(420));
const bool vcoh_input_ok = IN_RANGE(ref_ck, MHZ(2), MHZ(16));
const bool vcoh_output_ok = IN_RANGE(target_vco_ck, VCOH_MIN_FREQ, VCOH_MAX_FREQ);
/* Prefer VCOL if possible (lower power consumption) */
/* Otherwise, use VCOH if the configuration is achievable */
/* Illegal clock configuration for this hardware */
/** @brief Verifies clock is part of active clock configuration */

claude.label: not_needed_hw
claude.label_text: Not needed: different chip, device or board
claude.evidence: The H7 fix is about choosing the VCO operation mode (VCOL/VCOH, written with LL_RCC_PLLx_SetVCOOutputRange) together with the input range; per the commit message, the old logic "deduces" the operation mode from input range, which is wrong because "the valid input ranges depend on the selected VCO mode", and the new code also reads the per-product st,vcoh-frequency-range property. The WBA driver has no VCO operation mode at all: set_up_plls only calls get_vco_input_range and LL_RCC_PLL1_SetVCOInputRange, there is no get_vco_output_range and no SetVCOOutputRange call, and get_vco_input_range maps only 4-8 MHz and 8-16 MHz (no 1-2 MHz VCOL range). The repository's WBA PLL binding describes a single PLL with "an input frequency from 4 to 16 MHz" and one VCO range, "VCOx frequency range is 128 to 544 MHz", whereas the H7 PLL binding allows 1 to 16 MHz input and the st,vcoh-frequency-range property exists only in the H7 RCC binding (the WBA RCC binding has no such property). With a single VCO range, selecting the input range from ref_ck alone is correct on WBA, so the mode-deduction bug cannot occur there.

fix.subject: drivers: gpio: max149x6: propagate config path errors
fix.message:
drivers: gpio: max149x6: propagate config path errors

max14906_ch_func(), gpio_max14906_config(), and gpio_max14916_config()
ignore return values from lower level register update/write helpers.

This leads to reports of successful pin configuration even when SPI
transactions fail.

Fixed by propagating the first error (effectively forwarding SPI errors)
to the caller, with no behaviour change in success path.

Signed-off-by: Stan Verschuuren <stverschuuren@gmail.com>

In gpio_max14917.c the config function gpio_max14917_config() (line 238) makes no SPI or register call at all: the GPIO_OUTPUT case is only 'break;' (lines 259-260) and every other direction returns -ENOTSUP, so there is no helper return value to drop; the function has looked like this since the driver was added in 1489038f3b. fix.subject: drivers: audio: dmic_stm32_dfsdm: fix invalid Awd.Oversampling=0 default
fix.message:
drivers: audio: dmic_stm32_dfsdm: fix invalid Awd.Oversampling=0 default

HAL_DFSDM_ChannelInit() writes (Awd.Oversampling - 1) into the
CHAWSCDR.AWFOSR field and asserts that the ratio is in [1, 32].  The
static channel initializer in DMIC_DFSDM_CHAN_DEFINE() left
.Oversampling = 0, so:

  - in debug/asserts-enabled builds the HAL assert fires immediately
    from HAL_DFSDM_ChannelInit();
  - in release builds CHAWSCDR is programmed with a wrap-around value
    instead of a valid analog-watchdog oversampling ratio.

Default the static struct to a complete, valid configuration
(Oversampling = 1, FilterOrder = DFSDM_CHANNEL_FASTSINC_ORDER) so the
HAL contract is honoured before any runtime reconfiguration takes
place.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Cabé <benjamin@zephyrproject.org>
Assisted-by: Claude:opus-4.7

fix.subject: drivers: clock_control: stm32u5: fix EPOD booster prescaler
fix.message:
drivers: clock_control: stm32u5: fix EPOD booster prescaler

The EPOD booster clock is the PLL1 source clock divided by PLL1MBOOST;
PLL1M is not in its path (RM0456 Rev 7, RCC_PLL1CFGR in section 11.8.9,
p.526, and Figure 38, p.487). set_epod_booster() divides by PLL1M as
well, so with PLL1M > 1 and a source above 16 MHz it picks too small a
prescaler: blackpill_u585ci (25 MHz HSE, PLL1M 5) gets /1 and feeds the
booster 25 MHz, outside the 4 to 16 MHz of section 10.5.4 (p.410). The
pll_hse_fracn_160 scenario of the stm32u5_core clock test (16.78 MHz
HSE, PLL1M 2) gets /1 as well.

Leave PLL1M out of the computation. Build-tested only.

Assisted-by: Claude:claude-opus-5-5
Signed-off-by: YunHung Hua <oliverhua.us@gmail.com>

* Set EPOD clock prescaler based on PLL1 source freq
* (MSIS, HSI16 or HSE), taken before PLLM
* Booster clock frequency should be between 4 and 16MHz
* This is done in following steps:
* Read MSIS, HSI16 or HSE oscillator freq
* Divide it by the targeted freq (8MHz).
* Make sure value is not higher than 16
/* Configure the epod clock frequency between 4 and 16 MHz */
/* Enable EPOD booster and wait for booster ready flag set */

claude.label_text: Not needed: different chip, device or board
claude.evidence: The hunk is a real fix: the commit message says set_epod_booster() 'divides by PLL1M as well, so with PLL1M > 1 and a source above 16 MHz it picks too small a prescaler', and the fix leaves PLL1M out of the PLL1MBOOST computation. On U5 that code is compiled only under '#if defined(STM32_PLL_ENABLED)' (line 493) and is called from the PLL1 setup path (line 607), where it programs LL_RCC_SetPll1EPodPrescaler() (line 536). The U3 clock driver has no PLL at all: it never references STM32_PLL_ENABLED or STM32_PLL_M_DIVISOR, its SYSCLK can only be MSIS, HSE or HSI (lines 87-91 and 643-653), and the clocks node of dts/arm/st/u3/stm32u3.dtsi (from line 82) defines only hse, hsi, hsi48, msis, msik, lse and lsi, with no counterpart of the U5 'pll1: pll: pll' node of compatible st,stm32u5-pll-clock (stm32u5.dtsi line 141). The U3 booster is set up by enable_epod_booster() (line 336), which selects MSIS as the booster clock source with a fixed /1 prescaler through different LL calls (LL_RCC_SetEPODBoosterClkSource and LL_RCC_SetEPODBoosterClkPrescaler, lines 338-339), so there is no PLL1M divisor in its path to remove.

fix.subject: drivers: sensor: lsm6dsv16x: fix OOB odr_map index for high-accuracy ODR
fix.message:
drivers: sensor: lsm6dsv16x: fix OOB odr_map index for high-accuracy ODR

data->accel_freq and data->gyro_freq hold the full mode-encoded ODR
byte (mode in the upper nibble, e.g. 0x18 for HA01 500 Hz), so using
them directly as a column index into lsm6dsv16x_odr_map[3][13] reads
out of bounds for high-accuracy devicetree ODRs. Mask to the low
nibble, which is the actual CTRL ODR field; the mode nibble is already
handled via the row index.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Cabé <benjamin@zephyrproject.org>
Assisted-by: Claude:fable-5

Its lis2de12_odr_map (line 26) is a one-dimensional table read only inside lis2de12_freq_to_odr_val(), where the index is a loop counter bounded by ARRAY_SIZE (lines 32-33). data->accel_freq is only written (line 91) and is not read anywhere in drivers/sensor/st/lis2de12/, and there is no gyroscope field at all. fix.subject: drivers: sensor: max30009: fix NULL deref in flush_rtio error path
fix.message:
drivers: sensor: max30009: fix NULL deref in flush_rtio error path

max30009_flush_rtio is only called after the streaming request was
already completed with rtio_iodev_sqe_ok and data->sqe was set to
NULL, so calling rtio_iodev_sqe_err(data->sqe, -ENOMEM) on SQE
acquire failure dereferenced NULL. Drop any partially acquired SQE
with rtio_sqe_drop_all instead, matching the other error paths.

Signed-off-by: Benjamin Cabé <benjamin@zephyrproject.org>
Assisted-by: Claude:fable-5

claude.label: same_bug
claude.label_text: Flagged as a missed fix (written differently, so the script did not match it)
claude.evidence: The hunk is a real fix: per the commit message, max30009_flush_rtio() runs only after the streaming request 'was already completed with rtio_iodev_sqe_ok and data->sqe was set to NULL', so its SQE-acquire-failure branch 'dereferenced NULL'; the fix drops the partially acquired SQEs with rtio_sqe_drop_all() instead. The corresponding adxl367_fifo_flush_rtio() (line 36) is called in the same situation, from the SENSOR_STREAM_DATA_DROP branch of adxl367_process_status_cb() after 'data->sqe = NULL;' (lines 507 and 522-524). It never checks rtio_sqe_acquire() for NULL: it acquires five SQEs (lines 44, 49, 55, 66, 67) from an 8-entry pool (adxl367.c line 1182) and passes each straight to rtio_sqe_prep_tiny_write() or rtio_sqe_prep_callback() (lines 47 and 72), while rtio.h documents that rtio_sqe_acquire() returns NULL when no SQE is available and rtio_sqe_prep_tiny_write() starts with memset(sqe, 0, ...) (sqe.h line 641). So when the SQE pool is exhausted, adxl367 ends the same way max30009 did before the fix, with a NULL dereference in the flush path; the cause differs (no check at all, rather than a NULL request passed to rtio_iodev_sqe_err()), which is why confidence is medium and the port has to be adapted. Nothing ties the fix to hardware or configuration: both drivers use the same RTIO API, and the fix only changes how an SQE shortage is handled.

refs.quote: @retval NULL No subsmission queue event available

claude.title: adxl367_fifo_flush_rtio() uses RTIO submission entries without checking that they were acquired, so running out of them dereferences NULL in the FIFO flush path.
claude.summary: Commit 2abd8f6782 (2026-08-20) fixed max30009_flush_rtio(): when it could not acquire RTIO submission entries it reported the error on data->sqe, which is already NULL at that point, and crashed; it now drops the partially acquired entries with rtio_sqe_drop_all(), re-enables the interrupt and returns. The corresponding adxl367_fifo_flush_rtio() runs in the same situation (the DROP branch, after data->sqe has been cleared) but does not check rtio_sqe_acquire() at all: it takes five entries from an 8-entry pool and writes through each pointer straight away. If the pool is exhausted, adxl367 crashes with a NULL dereference instead of logging the failure, dropping the partial entries and re-enabling its interrupt. The patch cannot be copied line for line: adxl367 first needs the NULL checks, then the same rtio_sqe_drop_all() error path. The root cause is not identical to max30009 (no check at all, rather than a wrong pointer inside the check), and pool exhaustion is an uncommon condition, so a human should confirm that this counts as the same problem.

fix.subject: [bsp][n32] n32hxxx: add the H47x_48x/H49x timer support and cover the BSP with ci-attach
fix.message:
[bsp][n32] n32hxxx: add the H47x_48x/H49x timer support and cover the BSP with ci-attach

The N32H47x_48x and N32H49x series share drv_tim.c with N32H7xx, but only the
H7xx branch was ever implemented, so clock timer, LPTIM, PWM and pulse encoder
built to nothing on n32h487zgl7-evb and n32h497zgl7-evb.  This adds those
branches and gives all three boards a ci-attach entry set that actually
compiles what the drivers claim to support.

Drivers

  - drv_tim.c gains the H47x_48x/H49x clock-source and clock-enable branches,
    the ATIM/GTIM/BTIM instance tables and n32_tim_clock_freq_get(), which
    reads the real PCLK/HCLK/SYSCLK back from RCC rather than assuming one.
    ATIMCLKSEL is inverted between the two families and is handled as such.
  - drv_lptim.c derives its tick from the real LSI value instead of a
    hard-coded one, unlocks the backup domain before touching RCC, latches
    the prescaler, and returns -RT_EINVAL rather than clamping a bad rate.
  - drv_pwm.c and drv_pulse_encoder.c are extended to the H47x_48x/H49x
    instances; the H7xx encoder's update event is cleared through
    TIM_EnableUpdateEvt() because that family has no TIM_ConfigUpdateEvt().
  - config/{h47x_48x,h49x}/{tim,pwm,pulse_encoder,lptim}_config.h are new and
    enumerate the instances each series has, for the existing drivers to read.

Kconfig

Each board defines the timer menus in its own board/Kconfig, so that a
board's peripheral options live with the board and the shared driver
Kconfig stays series-neutral; libraries/N32_Drivers/drivers/Kconfig is
byte-identical to upstream/master.  All three copies enforce the mutual
exclusion drv_pulse_encoder.c documents (a timer instance enabled for both
clock timer and pulse encoder collides at link time on the shared ISR
symbol); N32H7xx's menus had none at all and are brought in line.

ci-attach

51 entries across the three boards (17/16/18).  h487 carries three NAND
entries - peripheral.nand, peripheral.nand_16b and peripheral.nand_large -
and h497 and h760 carry one each.  peripheral.nand_large exists because
drv_nand.c picks the row-address cycle count from pages_per_block *
block_count: 2 cycles up to 65536 pages, 3 up to 16777216, else 4.  Every
other NAND entry takes the Kconfig default 64 * 1024 = 65536, which lands
exactly on the first boundary, so the >= 3 and >= 4 arms were compiled by
nothing at all - it takes a geometry past the 24-bit row width to reach the
top rung.  The entry pins that geometry to arm them; it is not a claim about
the part on the board.

Fixes carried in the same series

  - drv_nand.c emitted its third row-address byte under `== 3`, so a 4-cycle
    part would set the count to 4 and then match no emitter, dropping the
    high row-address bytes outright.  The three guards are now >= 3 with the
    >= 4 byte added.  row_addr is uint32_t at all three sites.
  - timer_ctrl() wrote the prescaler straight to a 16-bit PSC field.
    TIM_ConfigPrescaler() neither masks nor validates, so any freq below
    timer_clock/65537 was truncated and the timer ran at an unrelated rate
    while timer->freq still recorded the requested one.  That window is
    reachable: both boards clock timers at 240 MHz, so the honest floor is
    ~3662 Hz while tim_config.h sets minfreq = 3000 and only [minfreq,
    maxfreq] is checked - 3000 Hz lands in PSC as 14463, about 16.6 kHz.
    Division by zero and any prescaler above 0xFFFF now return -RT_EINVAL.
    The H7xx branch had the identical truncation, so the same two guards
    are applied there too.
  - n32_tim_enable_clock() closed each new branch with RT_ASSERT(RT_TRUE).
    With RT_DEBUGING_ASSERT on, RT_ASSERT() expands to `if (!(EX))
    rt_assert_handler(...)`, so that guard could never fire: a timer
    matching none of the branch's instances enabled no clock at all and
    the caller went on to touch an unclocked peripheral's registers.  All
    three branches are now RT_FALSE.  The H7xx guard cannot fire today -
    every instance its config header can hand out is already in that
    branch's ladder - so fixing it arms the guard against a future
    instance added to the table but not the ladder, rather than changing
    any existing configuration.
  - h497's sdram entry asked for BSP_SDRAM_SIZE=32 while sdram_port.h
    documents the part as 8 MB and board/Kconfig declares `range 8 256` with
    `default 8`; the 32 came from h760, whose own default happens to be 32.
  - drv_hard_i2c.c had no init path at all for H47x_48x/H49x, leaving those
    series with an unconfigured controller; the SCL rate now travels in the
    config struct instead of being assumed.
  - drv_qspi.c and drv_spi.c indexed buffers longer than 65535 bytes with
    16-bit counters, which wraps at exactly 65536.
  - n32eth_cfg.h is added because the H7xx and H49x SDKs' eth.h include it
    but no package in the tree ships it.  It probes for the series headers
    because the SDK includes it before rtconfig.h can define SOC_SERIES_*,
    with a part-macro fallback for ARM Compiler 5, which has no
    __has_include() and is what every Keil project in this BSP uses.
  - n32h487zgl7-evb now builds with its real 8 MHz crystal; left at the
    header's 16 MHz default, RCC_GetClocksFreqValue() reports every clock at
    twice its value and the timer prescalers come out twice too large.
  - n32h760zil7-stb's timer menus had no mutual exclusion at all, so a timer
    instance could be enabled as both a clock timer and a pulse encoder; 24
    ISR symbols are defined by both drivers under those two guards, so only
    the linker would have caught it.  Its 14 PWM menus and its 14 encoder
    entries now carry the same guard as the two new boards', using the
    PWMn == PULSE_ENCODERN == instance n mapping that config/h7xx's
    pulse_encoder_config.h establishes.  On the PWM side that guard is a
    resource guard, not a link one: drv_pwm.c defines no ISRs.
  - the same board's LPTIM menu selected RT_USING_LPTIMER, which is not
    declared anywhere in the tree.  A select of an undeclared symbol is an
    implicit symbol and raises no diagnostic, so the line had never done
    anything; it is dropped, as the two new menus already do.  Three stm32
    boards still carry it and are left alone.

The H49x LPTIM EXTI lines needed the user manual rather than the SDK to
settle, and the manual sides with the driver: N32H49x maps EXTI line 21 to
the LPTIM1 wakeup event and line 22 to LPTIM2, which is what
n32_lptim_get_exti_line() returns.  The headers disagree only because
n32h49x_exti.h's EXTI_LINE16..24 block is a verbatim copy of
n32h47x_48x_exti.h's - that one carries on past line 24 and names 25/26 as
the LPTIM events with 21/22 as COMP1/COMP4 - while the H49x series has no
comparator in its SDK at all, so its copy of that text is stale.  The
driver states the reasoning in a comment rather than the bare value.

The H49x timer clock-source bits needed the user manual rather than the SDK
to settle.  For GTIM8/9/10 (RCC_CFG2 bit 27) h49x names the cleared case
RCC_GTIM_CLKSRC_SYSCLKDIV where h47x_48x names it RCC_GTIM_CLKSRC_PCLK, and
the manual sides with the driver's arithmetic: bit 27 selects SYSCLK, or
SYSCLK/(APB2 prescaler / 2) when that prescaler is engaged - the same rule
the driver writes from the HCLK side as PCLK2 doubled whenever PCLK2 is
below HCLK.  Both boards hold AHBPRES at RCC_SYSCLK_DIV1, so HCLK and SYSCLK
are the same 240 MHz and either spelling gives the same number.  The driver
tests the raw bit and not either family's constant, so the naming difference
never reaches the code.  The same chapter confirms bit 28's inversion, which
the ATIM branches already follow.

Verified: all three boards build from scratch under --strict (gcc -Werror)
with zero diagnostics; all 51 ci-attach entries build clean; the three
series were rebuilt after the assert fix, each through the --attach path
that compiles its branch (devices.timer on all three boards - h760's
default leaves BSP_USING_CLOCK_TIMER off, so drv_tim.c is not compiled by
it at all), rebuilt again after the Kconfig guards, whose
effect was checked by loading the tree with kconfiglib and confirming that
clock-timer ATIM1 with pulse encoder1 goes from satisfiable to unsatisfiable
while a non-colliding pair is left alone); the NAND row-address arms were
confirmed compiled by injecting #error markers and rebuilding through the
real --attach path; each board's committed .config and rtconfig.h reproduce
byte-for-byte from a fresh defconfig; and the CI clang-format gate reports
0 files / 0 lines.

claude.label: not_a_fix
claude.evidence: The commit message says it adds "the H47x_48x/H49x timer support" and that "drv_pwm.c and drv_pulse_encoder.c are extended to the H47x_48x/H49x instances"; the bug fixes it lists are in drv_nand.c and timer_ctrl(), not in drv_pwm.c. The first picked hunk replaces MAX_PERIOD with pwm_max_period_get(), which still returns MAX_PERIOD (65535) for every timer except GTIM1-4 under SOC_SERIES_N32H49x, where it returns 0xFFFFFFFF so the newly supported series can use its wider counter; for all previously supported timers the result is unchanged, and keeping ARR within 65535 is still a valid setting, so this extends the driver rather than correcting it. The second picked hunk wraps the PWM4 channel setup in #if defined(SOC_SERIES_N32H7xx) because only the n32 H7xx pwm_config.h defines a PWM4 (ATIM4) instance, and the same commit guards the PWM4 enum and table entries the same way. The at32 drv_pwm.c has no n32 series split: its PWM4_INDEX and BSP_USING_PWM3_CH4/PWM4_CHx lines match only as text, and its psc = period / MAX_PERIOD + 1 keeps ARR within 16 bits, consistent with its own MAX_PERIOD of 65535.

fix.subject: [bsp][n32] n32hxxx: add the H47x_48x/H49x timer support and cover the BSP with ci-attach
fix.message:
[bsp][n32] n32hxxx: add the H47x_48x/H49x timer support and cover the BSP with ci-attach

The N32H47x_48x and N32H49x series share drv_tim.c with N32H7xx, but only the
H7xx branch was ever implemented, so clock timer, LPTIM, PWM and pulse encoder
built to nothing on n32h487zgl7-evb and n32h497zgl7-evb.  This adds those
branches and gives all three boards a ci-attach entry set that actually
compiles what the drivers claim to support.

Drivers

  - drv_tim.c gains the H47x_48x/H49x clock-source and clock-enable branches,
    the ATIM/GTIM/BTIM instance tables and n32_tim_clock_freq_get(), which
    reads the real PCLK/HCLK/SYSCLK back from RCC rather than assuming one.
    ATIMCLKSEL is inverted between the two families and is handled as such.
  - drv_lptim.c derives its tick from the real LSI value instead of a
    hard-coded one, unlocks the backup domain before touching RCC, latches
    the prescaler, and returns -RT_EINVAL rather than clamping a bad rate.
  - drv_pwm.c and drv_pulse_encoder.c are extended to the H47x_48x/H49x
    instances; the H7xx encoder's update event is cleared through
    TIM_EnableUpdateEvt() because that family has no TIM_ConfigUpdateEvt().
  - config/{h47x_48x,h49x}/{tim,pwm,pulse_encoder,lptim}_config.h are new and
    enumerate the instances each series has, for the existing drivers to read.

Kconfig

Each board defines the timer menus in its own board/Kconfig, so that a
board's peripheral options live with the board and the shared driver
Kconfig stays series-neutral; libraries/N32_Drivers/drivers/Kconfig is
byte-identical to upstream/master.  All three copies enforce the mutual
exclusion drv_pulse_encoder.c documents (a timer instance enabled for both
clock timer and pulse encoder collides at link time on the shared ISR
symbol); N32H7xx's menus had none at all and are brought in line.

ci-attach

51 entries across the three boards (17/16/18).  h487 carries three NAND
entries - peripheral.nand, peripheral.nand_16b and peripheral.nand_large -
and h497 and h760 carry one each.  peripheral.nand_large exists because
drv_nand.c picks the row-address cycle count from pages_per_block *
block_count: 2 cycles up to 65536 pages, 3 up to 16777216, else 4.  Every
other NAND entry takes the Kconfig default 64 * 1024 = 65536, which lands
exactly on the first boundary, so the >= 3 and >= 4 arms were compiled by
nothing at all - it takes a geometry past the 24-bit row width to reach the
top rung.  The entry pins that geometry to arm them; it is not a claim about
the part on the board.

Fixes carried in the same series

  - drv_nand.c emitted its third row-address byte under `== 3`, so a 4-cycle
    part would set the count to 4 and then match no emitter, dropping the
    high row-address bytes outright.  The three guards are now >= 3 with the
    >= 4 byte added.  row_addr is uint32_t at all three sites.
  - timer_ctrl() wrote the prescaler straight to a 16-bit PSC field.
    TIM_ConfigPrescaler() neither masks nor validates, so any freq below
    timer_clock/65537 was truncated and the timer ran at an unrelated rate
    while timer->freq still recorded the requested one.  That window is
    reachable: both boards clock timers at 240 MHz, so the honest floor is
    ~3662 Hz while tim_config.h sets minfreq = 3000 and only [minfreq,
    maxfreq] is checked - 3000 Hz lands in PSC as 14463, about 16.6 kHz.
    Division by zero and any prescaler above 0xFFFF now return -RT_EINVAL.
    The H7xx branch had the identical truncation, so the same two guards
    are applied there too.
  - n32_tim_enable_clock() closed each new branch with RT_ASSERT(RT_TRUE).
    With RT_DEBUGING_ASSERT on, RT_ASSERT() expands to `if (!(EX))
    rt_assert_handler(...)`, so that guard could never fire: a timer
    matching none of the branch's instances enabled no clock at all and
    the caller went on to touch an unclocked peripheral's registers.  All
    three branches are now RT_FALSE.  The H7xx guard cannot fire today -
    every instance its config header can hand out is already in that
    branch's ladder - so fixing it arms the guard against a future
    instance added to the table but not the ladder, rather than changing
    any existing configuration.
  - h497's sdram entry asked for BSP_SDRAM_SIZE=32 while sdram_port.h
    documents the part as 8 MB and board/Kconfig declares `range 8 256` with
    `default 8`; the 32 came from h760, whose own default happens to be 32.
  - drv_hard_i2c.c had no init path at all for H47x_48x/H49x, leaving those
    series with an unconfigured controller; the SCL rate now travels in the
    config struct instead of being assumed.
  - drv_qspi.c and drv_spi.c indexed buffers longer than 65535 bytes with
    16-bit counters, which wraps at exactly 65536.
  - n32eth_cfg.h is added because the H7xx and H49x SDKs' eth.h include it
    but no package in the tree ships it.  It probes for the series headers
    because the SDK includes it before rtconfig.h can define SOC_SERIES_*,
    with a part-macro fallback for ARM Compiler 5, which has no
    __has_include() and is what every Keil project in this BSP uses.
  - n32h487zgl7-evb now builds with its real 8 MHz crystal; left at the
    header's 16 MHz default, RCC_GetClocksFreqValue() reports every clock at
    twice its value and the timer prescalers come out twice too large.
  - n32h760zil7-stb's timer menus had no mutual exclusion at all, so a timer
    instance could be enabled as both a clock timer and a pulse encoder; 24
    ISR symbols are defined by both drivers under those two guards, so only
    the linker would have caught it.  Its 14 PWM menus and its 14 encoder
    entries now carry the same guard as the two new boards', using the
    PWMn == PULSE_ENCODERN == instance n mapping that config/h7xx's
    pulse_encoder_config.h establishes.  On the PWM side that guard is a
    resource guard, not a link one: drv_pwm.c defines no ISRs.
  - the same board's LPTIM menu selected RT_USING_LPTIMER, which is not
    declared anywhere in the tree.  A select of an undeclared symbol is an
    implicit symbol and raises no diagnostic, so the line had never done
    anything; it is dropped, as the two new menus already do.  Three stm32
    boards still carry it and are left alone.

The H49x LPTIM EXTI lines needed the user manual rather than the SDK to
settle, and the manual sides with the driver: N32H49x maps EXTI line 21 to
the LPTIM1 wakeup event and line 22 to LPTIM2, which is what
n32_lptim_get_exti_line() returns.  The headers disagree only because
n32h49x_exti.h's EXTI_LINE16..24 block is a verbatim copy of
n32h47x_48x_exti.h's - that one carries on past line 24 and names 25/26 as
the LPTIM events with 21/22 as COMP1/COMP4 - while the H49x series has no
comparator in its SDK at all, so its copy of that text is stale.  The
driver states the reasoning in a comment rather than the bare value.

The H49x timer clock-source bits needed the user manual rather than the SDK
to settle.  For GTIM8/9/10 (RCC_CFG2 bit 27) h49x names the cleared case
RCC_GTIM_CLKSRC_SYSCLKDIV where h47x_48x names it RCC_GTIM_CLKSRC_PCLK, and
the manual sides with the driver's arithmetic: bit 27 selects SYSCLK, or
SYSCLK/(APB2 prescaler / 2) when that prescaler is engaged - the same rule
the driver writes from the HCLK side as PCLK2 doubled whenever PCLK2 is
below HCLK.  Both boards hold AHBPRES at RCC_SYSCLK_DIV1, so HCLK and SYSCLK
are the same 240 MHz and either spelling gives the same number.  The driver
tests the raw bit and not either family's constant, so the naming difference
never reaches the code.  The same chapter confirms bit 28's inversion, which
the ATIM branches already follow.

Verified: all three boards build from scratch under --strict (gcc -Werror)
with zero diagnostics; all 51 ci-attach entries build clean; the three
series were rebuilt after the assert fix, each through the --attach path
that compiles its branch (devices.timer on all three boards - h760's
default leaves BSP_USING_CLOCK_TIMER off, so drv_tim.c is not compiled by
it at all), rebuilt again after the Kconfig guards, whose
effect was checked by loading the tree with kconfiglib and confirming that
clock-timer ATIM1 with pulse encoder1 goes from satisfiable to unsatisfiable
while a non-colliding pair is left alone); the NAND row-address arms were
confirmed compiled by injecting #error markers and rebuilding through the
real --attach path; each board's committed .config and rtconfig.h reproduce
byte-for-byte from a fresh defconfig; and the CI clang-format gate reports
0 files / 0 lines.

lines: /* The driver owns the peripheral registers, so it pulls in the peripheral
* header itself instead of relying on board.h to have declared it.
/* All ATIM and GTIM timers on N32H7xx support 4 PWM output channels (CH1-CH4).
* BTIM1-4 are basic timers without PWM capability.
*   GTIMB1-3 -> pwm12-14 (general purpose, B bus, with complementary output)
/* Generate update event to apply immediately */
static rt_err_t drv_pwm_set_period(struct n32_pwm *pwm, struct rt_pwm_configuration *configuration)
static rt_err_t drv_pwm_set_pulse(struct n32_pwm *pwm, struct rt_pwm_configuration *configuration)
static rt_err_t drv_pwm_control(struct rt_device_pwm *device, int cmd, void *arg)
/* Converts the channel number to the channel number of Hal library */
/* Convert nanosecond to frequency and duty cycle. 1s = 1 * 1000 * 1000 * 1000 ns */
/* Convert nanosecond to frequency and duty cycle. 1s = 1 * 1000 * 1000 * 1000 ns */

claude.label: not_a_fix
claude.evidence: The commit message says it adds "the H47x_48x/H49x timer support" and that "drv_pwm.c and drv_pulse_encoder.c are extended to the H47x_48x/H49x instances"; the bug fixes it lists are in drv_nand.c and timer_ctrl(), not in drv_pwm.c. The three picked hunks all serve that extension: the first replaces an N32H7xx-only comment with N32_PWM_CMP_VALUE(), which casts to uint32_t only under SOC_SERIES_N32H49x and keeps the old uint16_t cast otherwise (the stm32 lines it matched are just the MIN_PERIOD/MIN_PULSE context); the second replaces MAX_PERIOD with pwm_max_period_get(), which still returns MAX_PERIOD for every timer except GTIM1-4 under SOC_SERIES_N32H49x; the third wraps the PWM4 channel setup in #if defined(SOC_SERIES_N32H7xx) because only the n32 H7xx pwm_config.h defines a PWM4 (ATIM4) instance. For the previously supported n32 series none of these changes behaviour, and keeping ARR within 65535 is still a valid setting, so they add support rather than correct an error. The stm32 drv_pwm.c has no n32 series split, writes the compare value through __HAL_TIM_SET_COMPARE without a 16-bit cast, and its psc = period / MAX_PERIOD + 1 is consistent with its own MAX_PERIOD of 65535.

fix.subject: fix:[stm32][lcd]Error in control call of lcd test function (#10040)
fix.message:
fix:[stm32][lcd]Error in control call of lcd test function (#10040)

* Optimize the lcd_test function to call it in thread to prevent the CLI environment from being unavailable after execution.

lines: rt_thread_t thread = rt_thread_create(thread_name, lcd_thread, lcd, 256, RT_THREAD_PRIORITY_MAX - 1, 10);

claude.label: missing
claude.evidence: The fix (title "Error in control call of lcd test function", body "Optimize the lcd_test function to call it in thread to prevent the CLI environment from being unavailable after execution") turned the stm32 lcd_test, an MSH command that looks up the "lcd" device and then loops forever, into a thread entry lcd_thread that a new lcd_test starts with rt_thread_create, and replaced lcd->parent.control with rt_device_control; the picked hunk is the start of the thread part. msh runs a command by calling it directly (*retp = cmd_func(argc, argv) in msh.c), so a command that never returns blocks the shell. In the ArtPi drv_spi_ili9488.c, ili9488_test is the same logic: it looks up "lcd" with rt_device_find (lines 1097-1098), draws some test content, then enters while (1) filling the framebuffer and calling lcd->parent.control with RTGRAPHIC_CTRL_RECT_UPDATE, and it is exported with MSH_CMD_EXPORT, so it never returns to the shell; nothing in the file starts it in its own thread, and DRV_DEBUG is defined in the file itself. The fix needs no hardware feature, and the same function also keeps the other half of the problem (not picked because the text differs): its lcd->parent.control calls cannot compile when RT_USING_DEVICE_OPS is on, because rtdef.h only declares the control member when that option is off, while this driver supports the option (device->ops = &lcd_ops). Only a debug shell command is affected.
claude.title: The ArtPi ILI9488 test shell command runs an endless drawing loop in the shell thread, so the shell is unusable after it is run.
claude.summary: On 2025-02-27, commit 50683295 changed lcd_test in the stm32 HAL drv_lcd.c so that its endless red/green/blue loop runs in its own thread (lcd_thread) and the shell command returns at once, and switched its screen-update calls to rt_device_control. The ArtPi drv_spi_ili9488.c has the same kind of test command, ili9488_test, which still looks up the "lcd" device and then loops forever in the caller's thread. If it is not fixed, running ili9488_test from msh blocks the shell until the board is reset; its lcd->parent.control calls also do not compile if RT_USING_DEVICE_OPS is enabled. The port needs rewriting rather than copying, because ili9488_test draws images and text before its loop and passes a rect_info argument, so the stack size for the new thread (256 bytes in the stm32 fix) must be checked; BSP_USING_SPI_LCD_ILI9488 is off in the board's default rtconfig.h.
claude.impact_note: Only the ili9488_test debug shell command is affected: running it never returns and leaves the msh shell unusable until reset (and its direct control calls break the build only with the non-default RT_USING_DEVICE_OPS option); normal LCD operation is unchanged.

claude.label: missing
claude.evidence: The fix (title "Error in control call of lcd test function", body "Optimize the lcd_test function to call it in thread to prevent the CLI environment from being unavailable after execution") turned the stm32 lcd_test, an MSH command that looks up the "lcd" device and then loops forever, into a thread entry lcd_thread that a new lcd_test starts with rt_thread_create after a NULL check, and replaced every lcd->parent.control call with rt_device_control. The WeAct drv_lcd_spi.c lcd_test is the same logic as the pre-fix code: the same rt_device_find lookup with no NULL check, a while (1) red/green/blue framebuffer fill, lcd->parent.control with RTGRAPHIC_CTRL_RECT_UPDATE after each color, and MSH_CMD_EXPORT(lcd_test, lcd_test); it only lacks the RGB888 branch, so the two RGB888-branch hunks have no separate counterpart while the other hunks map one to one. Because msh calls the command directly (*retp = cmd_func(argc, argv) in msh.c), the loop blocks the shell; and because rtdef.h declares the control member of struct rt_device only when RT_USING_DEVICE_OPS is off while this driver supports that option (device->ops = &lcd_ops), the direct calls cannot compile with it, whereas rt_device_control dispatches through dev->ops. The file defines DRV_DEBUG itself, nothing on this side runs the test in its own thread or uses another call path, and the fix depends on no hardware feature.
claude.title: The WeAct H750 lcd_test shell command still runs its endless loop in the shell thread and calls lcd->parent.control directly, the two problems fixed in the stm32 drv_lcd.c.
claude.summary: On 2025-02-27, commit 50683295 fixed lcd_test in bsp/stm32/libraries/HAL_Drivers/drivers/drv_lcd.c: the endless red/green/blue loop now runs in its own thread started by a new lcd_test that also checks the device lookup, and the screen-update calls go through rt_device_control. The WeAct board's drv_lcd_spi.c is a copy of the old code: its lcd_test looks up "lcd", loops forever in the caller's thread, calls lcd->parent.control three times and has no NULL check. If it is not fixed, running lcd_test from msh blocks the shell until the board is reset, and enabling RT_USING_DEVICE_OPS makes this file fail to compile because struct rt_device then has no control member. The command is built by default on this board (BSP_USING_LCD_SPI and FINSH_USING_MSH are set in its rtconfig.h), but only a debug command is affected.
claude.impact_note: Only the lcd_test debug shell command is affected: running it never returns and leaves the msh shell unusable until reset, and its direct control calls break the build only with the non-default RT_USING_DEVICE_OPS option; normal LCD operation is unchanged.

claude.label: missing

The thread part (the first hunk and the new lcd_test in the last hunk) does not apply here: the tkm32F499 lcd_test fills red, green and blue once each and returns 0, and it already checks the rt_device_find result for RT_NULL. The control-call hunks do apply: lcd_test (lines 272, 279, 286) and the non-debug helper Lcd_ColorBox (line 159) call lcd->parent.control directly, while this driver supports RT_USING_DEVICE_OPS (device->ops = &lcd_ops) and rtdef.h declares the control member of struct rt_device only when that option is off, so the file cannot compile with it, the same failure the stm32 lcd_test had; rt_device_control dispatches through dev->ops in that configuration. claude.title: The tkm32F499 LCD driver calls lcd->parent.control directly, which does not compile when RT_USING_DEVICE_OPS is enabled; the stm32 drv_lcd.c fix replaced the same call with rt_device_control.
claude.summary: On 2025-02-27, commit 50683295 fixed the stm32 drv_lcd.c test command by replacing its direct lcd->parent.control calls with rt_device_control and by moving its endless loop into a separate thread. The tkm32F499 drv_lcd.c still calls lcd->parent.control in Lcd_ColorBox, which is built whenever BSP_USING_LCD is set, and three times in lcd_test, although the driver itself has an RT_USING_DEVICE_OPS registration path; struct rt_device has no control member in that configuration, so the file fails to compile there. The thread part of the fix does not apply, because this lcd_test draws each color once and returns, and it already checks the device lookup for NULL. If it is not fixed, the only effect is that this LCD driver cannot be built with RT_USING_DEVICE_OPS enabled (default off); BSP_USING_LCD is also off in the board's default rtconfig.h.

fix.subject: [bsp][drv_gpio] fix the error code return when pin number is illegal
fix.message: [bsp][drv_gpio] fix the error code return when pin number is illegal

lines: static rt_ssize_t gd32_pin_read(rt_device_t dev, rt_base_t pin)
static void ht32_pin_mode(rt_device_t dev, rt_base_t pin, rt_uint8_t mode)
static void ht32_pin_write(rt_device_t dev, rt_base_t pin, rt_uint8_t value)
static rt_ssize_t ht32_pin_read(rt_device_t dev, rt_base_t pin)

claude.label: missing
claude.evidence: The commit "[bsp][drv_gpio] fix the error code return when pin number is illegal" changed pin_read in about 50 BSP GPIO drivers so that an unknown pin returns -RT_EINVAL instead of a pin level; in the gd32 risc-v driver the picked hunk turns "return value;" (value preset to PIN_LOW) into "return -RT_EINVAL;" after get_pin() returns RT_NULL. The ht32 drv_gpio.c ht32_pin_read is the same pre-fix logic: it presets value = PIN_LOW, calls get_pin(pin), and on RT_NULL returns value, so an illegal pin reads as low and the caller cannot see the error. Its return type is already rt_ssize_t, the same as the pin_read op in dev_pin.h and rt_pin_read, which passes the driver's value straight back, so nothing prevents returning -RT_EINVAL; the fix uses no hardware feature. The other lines the script matched (get_pin checks in pin_mode, pin_write and the irq functions) are only shared lookup context; the fix concerns the return value in pin_read. The ht32 driver was added on 2024-04-17, after the 2024-03-24 fix, and has not been changed since.

refs.quote: static rt_ssize_t ht32_pin_read(rt_device_t dev, rt_base_t pin)

claude.title: The HT32 GPIO driver returns PIN_LOW instead of an error code when asked to read an illegal pin number.
claude.summary: On 2024-03-24, commit 6a9c42a1 changed pin_read in about 50 BSP GPIO drivers, including the gd32 risc-v one, so that an illegal pin number returns -RT_EINVAL instead of a pin level. The HT32 BSP was added on 2024-04-17 with ht32_pin_read still written the old way: when get_pin() finds no entry it returns the preset PIN_LOW. If it is not fixed, rt_pin_read on an invalid pin silently reports a low level, and callers cannot tell a wrong pin number from a real low input. The change is one line and uses nothing specific to the HT32 hardware.
claude.impact_note: Only reads of a pin number that is not in the pin table are affected: they report PIN_LOW instead of returning -RT_EINVAL, so callers that pass valid pins see no change.

fix.subject: [bsp][nxp][mcxa153] fix compiling problem
fix.message: [bsp][nxp][mcxa153] fix compiling problem

lines: * 2024-08-1      hywing       The first version for MCXA
* 2019-07-15     yandld      The first version for MCXN

claude.label: not_applicable
claude.label_text: Fix does not apply to the copy
claude.evidence: The commit "[bsp][nxp][mcxa153] fix compiling problem" renamed the driver's own DMA_MAX_TRANSFER_COUNT (32767) to DMA_MAX_TRANSFER_SIZE in the mcxa drv_spi.c; at that commit the MCXA153 SDK header fsl_lpspi_edma.h (driver version 2.4.4), which drv_spi.c includes just before its definition, itself defines DMA_MAX_TRANSFER_COUNT 0x7FFFU, so the rename only removes that name clash and changes no value (0x7FFF = 32767). The mcxn drv_spi.c has the same include and definition (lines 14 and 16), but the MCXN236 and MCXN947 copies of fsl_lpspi_edma.h that the repository held (driver version 2.0.0 at the fix commit, 2.1.0 and 2.1.1 up to commit 27430ca7, which moved the SDK out of the tree in 2025-05) do not define DMA_MAX_TRANSFER_COUNT, so on mcxn the macro clashes with nothing. The problem therefore comes from the SDK version used for the MCXA153 part, not from the shared driver logic. At the pinned commit both BSPs take the SDK from the external package selected by PKG_USING_NXP_MCX_SERIES_DRIVER (version "latest"), which the repository does not hold, so the current MCXN header cannot be checked and confidence is only medium; even if a newer header defined the macro, its value would be the same 32767 and nothing at run time would change.

fix.subject: [BSP][NXP] Add new features of I2C DMA, CAN, SPI, DWT and SDIO for RT1180 (#11715)
fix.message:
[BSP][NXP] Add new features of I2C DMA, CAN, SPI, DWT and SDIO for RT1180 (#11715)

* updated template files, conifg files and script files to support hypperram, multicore kickoff, rpmsg-lite, netc, cherryusb and ethercat.

* updated different link files of GCC, IAR and KEIL, for supporting multicore kick-off and different loading methods

* Updated .ini files to support debugging in keil. And updeated .mac files to support deugging in iar.

* Updated template files, conifg files and script files of CM7 to support hypperram, multicore kickoff, rpmsg-lite, netc, cherryusb and ethercat.

* Updated different link files of GCC, IAR and KEIL of CM7 project, for supporting multicore kick-off and different loading methods.

* Modify LittleFS to use the last 1 MB of flash and update CM7 support for LittleFS on QSPI flash.

* Updated different link files of loading to hyperram.

* Updated .ini files of CM7 to support debugging in keil. And updeated .mac files of CM7 to support deugging in iar.

* Remove Keil projects and keep templates only.

* Remove RAMFUNC due to IAR compilation issues, and use linker configuration to place all flash operation code in RAM.

* Add related code to support kick-offing CM7 and rpmsg-lite.

* Add codes to support cherryUSB for CM33 and CM7.

* Add mnt.c to support littleFS for CM7.

* Add codes to support etherCAT for CM7.

* Add codes to support USART12 for RT1180.

* Modify the drv_uart_v2.c to fix some bug to make it can work in CM33, but still cannot work in CM7. Will continue to update in next version.

* Updated README with both Chinese and English versions.

* Move the EtherCAT code into the packages\nxp-imxrt-sdk-latest.

* Remove EtherCAT-related sources, keep only SConscript.

* updated ci.attachconfig.yml for cm33 and cm7 projects.

* Fixed BSP_ROOT path error in rtconfig.py.

claude.label_text: Fix does not apply to the copy
claude.evidence: The hunk un-comments the 0x20000000-0x20080000 range in the bounce-buffer condition of _mmc_request, so that buffers in i.MX RT tightly coupled memory are copied through an aligned heap buffer before USDHC DMA; the fixed line's comment gives the reason: 'DTCM/System TCM - not DMA-accessible'. The imx6ull-smart copy still has this range commented out at line 464 in the same function, but this BSP (ARCH_ARM_CORTEX_A7 with MMU) has no TCM at that address: board.h documents the memory map as OCRAM at 0x0090_0000 plus peripheral blocks at 0x0200_0000-0x022F_FFFF, and board.c maps 0x00000000-0x80000000 as DEVICE_MEM with normal memory only from 0x80000000 (or from KERNEL_VADDR_START 0xc0000000 under RT_USING_SMART). The system heap is set up in DDR between __bss_end and HEAP_END (0x80000000 + 64 MB, or KERNEL_VADDR_START + 16 MB), so no data buffer is expected in the 0x20000000 window the fix targets. The fix depends on the i.MX RT TCM address layout, which this board does not have; the ITCM check that is already present there is likewise a leftover from the i.MX RT driver.

lines: /* user does not specify hdr index,set hdr_bank from RX MB 1 */

/* RX MB index from 1 to 32,hdr index 0~31 map RX MB index 1~32. */

claude.label: missing
claude.evidence: The picked hunks change '1 << i' and '1 << index' to '1U << i' and '1U << index' in the RT_CAN_CMD_SET_FILTER branch of can_control; the commit message bullet says 'fix: use unsigned shift to avoid UB in drv_can.c'. The bit index runs from 0 to 31 (comment 'hdr index 0~31 map RX MB index 1~32'), and shifting the int constant 1 into bit 31 is undefined behaviour in C, which the unsigned literal avoids. The mcxn copy has the same can_control filter code with the same static rt_uint32_t filter_mask bitmap, the same 0..31 search loop at line 250, and the unchanged signed shifts at lines 252 and 276 (plus line 261 for a user-given hdr_bank, which the source commit also changed); nothing in the copy keeps the index below 31 before shifting, and the CAN core passes the filter request to the driver before any hdr_bank range check. The fix needs only a 1U literal, so no hardware or SDK dependency could make it inapplicable; with common compilers the signed shift still yields 0x80000000, so the runtime result most likely stays the same.

refs.quote: /* RX MB index from 1 to 32,hdr index 0~31 map RX MB index 1~32. */

claude.title: The MCXN CAN driver tracks used filter slots with signed shifts (1 << i, 1 << index), which are undefined in C when the slot index reaches 31.
claude.summary: On 2026-08-21 commit 6ea68279 changed the i.MX RT CAN driver to use unsigned shifts (1U << i, 1U << index, 1U << item->hdr_bank) when it records which receive mailboxes already have a filter, to avoid undefined behaviour. The MCXN CAN driver is a copy of the same filter code and still uses 1 << i and 1 << index at lines 252 and 276, and 1 << item->hdr_bank at line 261. When filter slot 31 is searched or used, the shift moves a 1 into the sign bit of an int, which C leaves undefined; in practice compilers give 0x80000000, so filters most likely keep working. The same one-character change per line carries over unchanged.
claude.impact_note: Shifting 1 into bit 31 of a signed int is undefined in C, but common compilers produce 0x80000000, so the filter bitmap most likely behaves the same once fixed.

fix.subject: bsp: fm33lc026: Fix GPIO IRQ map lookup
fix.message:
bsp: fm33lc026: Fix GPIO IRQ map lookup

Keep pin2irqindex within the pin_irq_map bounds and handle the first map entry without reading index -1. Pass encoded pin values to the IRQ map lookup path, and validate the lookup result before indexing the map.

Generated-by: OpenAI Codex
Signed-off-by: Old-Ding <35417409+Old-Ding@users.noreply.github.com>

claude.label: not_applicable
claude.label_text: Fix does not apply to the copy
claude.evidence: The picked hunk changes the PIN_IRQ_DISABLE branch of fm33_pin_irq_enable from get_pin_irq_map(PIN_STPIN(pin)) to get_pin_irq_map(pin); the commit message says 'Pass encoded pin values to the IRQ map lookup path'. That is right for fm33lc026 because its get_pin_irq_map(rt_base_t pin) calls pin2irqindex(pin), which compares the encoded pin number against a pin_irq_map that holds encoded pin numbers such as {3, FL_GPIO_EXTI_LINE_0}. In the n32hxxx driver, get_pin_irq_map(uint32_t pinbit) instead calls bit2bitno(pinbit), and its pin_irq_map is indexed by pin bit position ({ GPIO_PIN_0, EXTI_LINE0, EXTI0_IRQn }, ...), so it expects the bit mask that PIN_STPIN(pin) produces; the enable branch of the same function also uses bit2bitno(PIN_STPIN(pin)). Line 397 only has the same text as the pre-fix fm33lc026 line, not the same logic: there PIN_STPIN(pin) is the correct argument, and passing the encoded pin would break the lookup.

fix.message:
[bsp/nxp/mcx/mcxa] Fix UART clock configuration type mismatch

Fixed implicit type conversion warning in UART driver by correctly
separating clock_name_t and clock_attach_id_t enum types.

Changes:
- Use kCLOCK_Fro12M (clock_name_t) for clock_src field
- Keep kFRO12M_to_LPUARTx (clock_attach_id_t) for clock_attach_id field
- Fix mcx_getc() to use correct status flag kLPUART_RxDataRegFullFlag

This resolves the compiler warning:
"implicit conversion from 'int' to 'clock_name_t' changes value from 16777216 to 0"

Signed-off-by: Yucai Liu 1486344514@qq.com

claude.label: missing
claude.evidence: The picked hunk replaces kLPUART_RxDataRegFullInterruptEnable with kLPUART_RxDataRegFullFlag in mcx_getc, where the constant is ANDed with the value returned by LPUART_GetStatusFlags(); the commit message lists 'Fix mcx_getc() to use correct status flag kLPUART_RxDataRegFullFlag'. The mcxe copy has the identical mcx_getc check at line 163, and elsewhere uses kLPUART_RxDataRegFullInterruptEnable as an interrupt-enable mask (lines 136 and 141), so testing the status word with it is the same mistake; the status-flag constants the fix relies on are already used by the mcxe driver (kLPUART_TxDataRegEmptyFlag in mcx_putc at line 153), so nothing makes the fix inapplicable. The MCX SDK header comes from an external package (CONFIG_PKG_USING_NXP_MCX_SERIES_DRIVER=y) and is not in the repository; the only in-tree NXP LPUART header (imx91 SDK) defines the enable constant as LPUART_CTRL_RIE_MASK and the flag as LPUART_STAT_RDRF_MASK and documents both as bit 21, so the old check most likely tests the right bit by coincidence and the runtime result most likely stays the same.

refs.quote: kLPUART_RxDataRegFullInterruptEnable = (LPUART_CTRL_RIE_MASK), /*!< Receiver data register full. bit 21 */

claude.title: The MCXE UART driver's mcx_getc checks for received data with the interrupt-enable constant kLPUART_RxDataRegFullInterruptEnable instead of the status flag kLPUART_RxDataRegFullFlag.
claude.summary: On 2025-10-21 commit 982e52e2 fixed the MCXA UART driver so that mcx_getc tests the receive status with the status flag kLPUART_RxDataRegFullFlag instead of the interrupt-enable constant kLPUART_RxDataRegFullInterruptEnable. The MCXE UART driver is a copy of that code and still has the old check at line 163. In the NXP LPUART header that is in the repository (imx91 SDK) both constants are documented as bit 21, so the check most likely works by coincidence today; if the MCX SDK gave them different values, mcx_getc would miss received bytes or read when nothing has arrived. The MCX SDK comes from an external package that is not in the repository, so the values for MCXE could not be confirmed. The fix is a one-word replacement.
claude.impact_note: The in-tree NXP LPUART header documents both constants as bit 21, so the wrong constant most likely tests the same status bit; the MCX SDK header itself is not in the repository to confirm this.

claude.label: missing
claude.evidence: The picked hunk replaces the plain assignments 'qspi_device->enter_qspi_mode = enter_qspi_mode;' and 'qspi_device->exit_qspi_mode = exit_qspi_mode;' in rt_hw_qspi_device_attach with explicit casts to void (*)(struct rt_qspi_device *); the commit message says 'fix: resolve QSPI compilation error' and 'Fix function pointer type mismatch between drv_qspi.h and rt_qspi_device'. The at32 driver has the same function with the same parameter types void (*enter_qspi_mode)() and void (*exit_qspi_mode)() (drv_qspi.c line 426, drv_qspi.h line 36) and stores them without a cast at lines 443-444 into struct rt_qspi_device members declared as void (*enter_qspi_mode)(struct rt_qspi_device *device) in dev_spi.h, so it has exactly the mismatch the commit names. With a compiler that treats '()' as '(void)', as C23 does, these assignments are between incompatible pointer types, so the toolchain that broke the STM32 file would also break this file whenever BSP_USING_QSPI is enabled (offered in the at32f435/437/455/456/457 board Kconfig); both BSP families build with GCC without an explicit -std flag. The fix needs nothing hardware-specific; only the build is affected, not the generated code.
claude.title: The AT32 QSPI driver stores the enter/exit QSPI-mode callbacks, declared as void (*)(), into rt_qspi_device members of type void (*)(struct rt_qspi_device *) without a cast, the same mismatch that broke the STM32 QSPI build.
claude.summary: On 2025-12-17 commit 99a25459 fixed a QSPI compilation error in the STM32 driver by casting the enter_qspi_mode and exit_qspi_mode callbacks to void (*)(struct rt_qspi_device *) before storing them in struct rt_qspi_device. The AT32 QSPI driver has the same rt_hw_qspi_device_attach with the same void (*)() parameters and still stores them without a cast at lines 443-444. With a compiler that treats '()' as '(void)', as C23 does, these are incompatible pointer assignments, so enabling BSP_USING_QSPI on an AT32 board would most likely fail to build with the same toolchain that broke the STM32 build. Runtime behaviour does not change; the exact compiler from issue #11036 is not visible in the repository.
claude.impact_note: Only decides whether drv_qspi.c compiles with a compiler that rejects the mismatched function-pointer assignment; the stored callback and runtime behaviour are the same.

lines: static rt_ssize_t spixfer(struct rt_spi_device* device, struct rt_spi_message* message)
* Attach the spi device to SPI bus, this function must be used after initialization.
rt_err_t rt_hw_spi_device_attach(const char *bus_name, const char *device_name, rt_base_t cs_pin)
static rt_uint32_t spixfer(struct rt_spi_device* device, struct rt_spi_message* message)

claude.label: not_applicable
claude.label_text: Fix does not apply to the copy
claude.evidence: The picked hunks change spixfer to read device->parent.user_data as a pin number and drive CS with rt_pin_write, because at the fix commit the arm driver's own rt_hw_spi_device_attach(bus_name, device_name, rt_base_t cs_pin) called rt_spi_bus_attach_device(..., (void *)cs_pin), while spixfer cast user_data to struct gd32_spi_cs * and dereferenced it. The risc-v drv_spi.c still has the pre-fix spixfer lines (267, 276, 375), but the whole file contains only gd32_spi_init, spi_configure, spixfer and rt_hw_spi_init with no attach helper, and its drv_spi.h exports struct gd32_spi_cs (GPIOx, GPIO_Pin) and declares no rt_hw_spi_device_attach. None of the three risc-v boards (gd32vf103r-start, gd32vf103v-eval, gd32vw553h-eval) attaches an SPI device in main.c or board.c, so the only contract the risc-v driver offers is that callers pass a struct gd32_spi_cs pointer as user_data, which spixfer reads consistently. The mismatch the fix repairs comes from the pin-number attach helper that the risc-v side does not have, and copying the fix there would break the struct-based contract its header advertises.

fix.subject: [bsp][esp32-c6] add ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1 support (#11836)
fix.message:
[bsp][esp32-c6] add ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1 support (#11836)

* [bsp][esp32-c6] add ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1 support

Add bsp/ESP/ESP32_C6. Default image is GPIO, UART0 and ADC. The C6 IDF sources are not in RT-Thread-packages/esp-idf yet.

* [bsp][esp32-c6] fix CI format, C6 package and CH32V203 D6 build

clang-format the files the format check rejected. Fetch the C6 scons
branch when the downloaded ESP-IDF package has no C6 target. Patch the
CH32V20x SDK under libraries so a D6 build no longer calls Exit().

* [bsp][esp32-c6] fetch mbedtls and stop pkgs from pulling the C6 branch

* [bsp][esp32-c6] rebuild CI against the package branch tip

* [bsp][esp32-c6] rebuild CI against the strict-mode package tip

* [bsp][esp32-c6] fix the reviewed ADC, math and package pin bugs

Keep the IDF tree on the reviewed commit, and stop the ADC and critical-section paths from reporting success when they did not.

* [bsp][esp32-c6] reserve stuck interrupt lines and lock ADC

CPU lines 3 and 4 never latch an enable, so copying the handler left the non-IRAM mask on the old line. Reserve those lines and let the allocator write the mask and the route together. The C6 oneshot registers are shared, so one mutex covers enable and convert.

* [bsp][esp32-c6] list the peripherals this board actually runs

GPIO, UART0 and ADC1 have been read on the DevKitC-1. Radios and the untested buses stay marked unsupported.

* [bsp][esp32-c6] keep SPI unsupported after the loopback mismatch

GPIO7 shorted to GPIO2 returned 0xA5000000 for a sent 0xA5, so the table does not mark SPI supported.

---------

fix.message: fix[stm32[SDMMC]: Optimize SDMMC timeout handling and clock divider

lines: LOG_E("L:%d F:%s mmcsd alloc host fail");
host->valid_ocr = 0X00FFFF80;/* The voltage range supported is 1.65v-3.6v */
* @brief  This function get stm32 sdio clock.
LOG_E("L:%d F:%s mmcsd alloc host fail");
host->valid_ocr = 0X00FFFF80;/* The voltage range supported is 1.65v-3.6v */
* @param  BufferSRC: pointer to the source buffer

claude.label: missing
claude.evidence: The commit message is 'fix[stm32[SDMMC]: Optimize SDMMC timeout handling and clock divider', but the picked hunks do not touch the timeout or divider code; the only part with a behavioural effect is the two LOG_E calls in sdio_host_create, whose old strings 'L:%d F:%s malloc rthw_sdio fail' and 'L:%d F:%s mmcsd alloc host fail' contain %d and %s but pass no arguments, while LOG_E expands (include/rtdbg.h) to rt_kprintf(fmt, ...), a varargs printf that reads an int and a char pointer that were never passed. The apm32 sdio_host_create has both calls unchanged at lines 632 and 640, in the same rt_malloc and mmcsd_alloc_host failure branches as the stm32 code before the fix, and its drv_log.h sets DBG_LVL to DBG_INFO, so LOG_E is compiled in whenever debug output is enabled. The other picked parts do not apply: apm32 already defaults clk_get to apm32_sdio_clk_get at line 647; max_blk_size/max_blk_count of 512 make no runtime difference because the core (dev_block.c line 392) caps each request at the smaller of max_dma_segs*max_seg_size and max_blk_count*max_blk_size, and max_seg_size is SDIO_BUFF_SIZE, with rthw_sdio_request also asserting size <= SDIO_BUFF_SIZE; and rthw_sdio_irq_update(host, 1) is the same as passing RT_TRUE. So the candidate counts as missing only for the two format strings, which only matter on an allocation failure during SDIO init.

refs.quote: LOG_E("L:%d F:%s mmcsd alloc host fail");

claude.title: The apm32 SDIO driver's two allocation-failure error messages contain %d and %s but pass no arguments, so printing them reads values that were never passed.
claude.summary: In commit e45e52d1 (committed 2026-04-14) the stm32 SDMMC driver changed two error messages in sdio_host_create to drop the 'L:%d F:%s' prefix; the calls pass no arguments for those placeholders. The apm32 drv_sdio.c has the same host-creation code and still has both old messages at lines 632 and 640, in the branches taken when rt_malloc or mmcsd_alloc_host fails. If either allocation fails while debug output is enabled, rt_kprintf reads an integer and a string pointer that were never passed, so the message comes out as garbage and the %s may read from an arbitrary address. The rest of the stm32 change (clk_get default, block count limit, RT_TRUE) does not need porting: apm32 already has the clk_get default, and the SDIO core already limits each transfer to SDIO_BUFF_SIZE. A related call at line 621 also has more placeholders than arguments, but it was not part of this candidate.
claude.impact_note: The bad format strings are only reached when rt_malloc or mmcsd_alloc_host fails during SDIO init, where the driver already gives up and returns RT_NULL, so the effect is a garbage error message (at worst a fault while printing it) on a path that has already failed.

lines: * @brief  This function get order from sdio.
/* Waiting for data to be sent to completion */
* @brief  This function get order from sdio.

claude.label: not_a_fix
claude.evidence: The picked hunks are (1) a new helper stm32_sdio_clk_get() that returns SDIO_CLOCK_FREQ, which the fixed driver only uses as a fallback when the descriptor's clk_get pointer is NULL, and (2)/(3) a swap of the whole-cache SCB_CleanInvalidateDCache() for buffer-range rt_hw_cpu_dcache_ops() calls on cache_buf around the IDMA transfer. Neither corrects a behavioural error: RT_HW_CACHE_FLUSH maps to SCB_CleanDCache_by_Addr on cache_buf, so the old whole-cache clean+invalidate already covered everything the new range calls do and the change only narrows cache maintenance (a speed-up), and the commit message ("Optimize SDMMC timeout handling and clock divider") does not mention cache handling at all. The helper has nothing to attach to here: this driver's rthw_sdio_iocfg() never calls a clk_get pointer and takes the clock directly from SDIO_CLOCK_FREQ. The commit's timeout and divider changes are not among the picked hunks; this driver already rounds the divider up (line 334) and keeps a loop-count data wait (line 221), which this candidate does not cover.

claude.label: missing
claude.evidence: The picked hunks change the PM callbacks wdt_pm_suspend, wdt_pm_frequency_change and usbhost_pm_suspend from int to rt_err_t (commit message: "Fix compilation issues with bsp of nuvoton series") and move the opening brace of the NU_USBHOST_MUTEX_INIT/LOCK/UNLOCK macros to the next line, which is formatting only. The return-type part is a build fix: since bceb6635 (July 2024) struct rt_device_pm_ops declares suspend and frequency_change as rt_err_t (pm.h line 138), rt_err_t is rt_base_t, i.e. rt_int32_t, which is int32_t in GCC builds because the newlib SConscript defines RT_USING_LIBC, so it need not be int, and initializing these members with int-returning functions is an incompatible function-pointer initialization. The m460 drv_wdt.c (prototypes at lines 104 and 106, definitions at 135 and 196, stored at line 125) and drv_usbhost.c (line 810, stored at line 857) still have exactly the pre-fix int callbacks inside the same RT_USING_PM blocks, so an m460 build with RT_USING_PM on gets the same diagnostic the commit removed from m480; nothing chip-specific is involved and the fixed m480 drv_wdt.c (line 132) shows the target form. Every callback returns (int)RT_EOK, so run-time behaviour is the same, the shipped numaker-iot-m467 config leaves RT_USING_PM off, no m460 drv_*.c calls rt_system_pm_init (only the m031, m2354 and m480 drv_clk.c do), and the repository does not show whether the original diagnostic was an error or only a warning, hence medium confidence and light impact.

claude.title: The M460 watchdog and USB host drivers still declare their PM callbacks as returning int, while struct rt_device_pm_ops now expects rt_err_t, so a build with RT_USING_PM gets the incompatible function-pointer initialization that commit e7e44ec fixed in the m031, m2354 and m480 copies.
claude.summary: On 2024-09-29 commit e7e44ec ("Fix compilation issues with bsp of nuvoton series") changed wdt_pm_suspend, wdt_pm_frequency_change and usbhost_pm_suspend in the m031, m2354 and m480 libraries from int to rt_err_t, to match struct rt_device_pm_ops, whose suspend and frequency_change members became rt_err_t in July 2024. The m460 library still declares and defines these callbacks as int (drv_wdt.c lines 104, 106, 135, 196; drv_usbhost.c line 810) and stores them in the same struct inside its RT_USING_PM blocks. With RT_USING_PM enabled the compiler reports an incompatible function-pointer initialization, which stops the build on compilers that reject it and is a warning on others. Behaviour at run time does not change because every callback returns RT_EOK; the shipped m467 configurations leave RT_USING_PM off, and the repository does not show whether the original problem was an error or only a warning.
claude.impact_note: Only decides whether the RT_USING_PM build of these drivers compiles cleanly; every callback returns (int)RT_EOK, so the PM core sees the same value either way.
